sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Wamani** ​(*wamani*) — ‌Sacred Mountain ‌· ​The falcon ​— ​belongs to ​the Incan ​tradition, ‌where it ​is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Sacred ‌Mountain". The ​name ‌means "The ​falcon"[^1].

**Wamani** ​is ​the Andean ​sacred ​mountain made ‌person: the ​tutelary ‌peak of ​a ‌province, ancestor ​of its ‌people, ​and keeper ‌of ​the springs ​that descend ‌from ‌its snowfields. ‌In ​the Inca ​world every ‌region ​had its ​wamani, ‌and the ​covenant between ​community ‌and mountain ​— ‌offerings for ​water, harvest, ​and ​protection — ​remains ‌alive in ‌Andean religion ​today.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ​the ​canonical scholarly ‌spelling **Wamani** ‌and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/wamani/). The ​displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*wamani* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sources.citation: Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo, Book 13 (1653).
Martín de Murúa, Historia general del Piru (1616).
Brian S. Bauer, The Sacred Landscape of the Inca (1998).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives ​for this ​name; ​**Wamani** ​is a ​scholarly ‌transliteration ​of the ​reconstructed ‌spoken ​form. Etymologically ‌the ​name ‌means "The ​falcon"[^1].

​The canonical ​spelling ​**Wamani** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly ‌romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form *wamani* ‌contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ​no ‌lost diacritics ‌or ‌encoding transition ​is ​claimed. ‌The editorial ​work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and provenance, ​and ​keep ​the original ‌evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**w** ​→ **W** ​— ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ‌**m** ​→ **m** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** ‌— ‌Same
- **n** ​→ ​**n** ​— Same
- ​**i** ‌→ ‌**i** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/wamani/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**wamani** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Wamani.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Wamani" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Wamani" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"wamani" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Wamani ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Wamani ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Wamani ‌place ​sacred mountain ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Wamani appears ‌in ​incan ‌tradition as ​sacred ​mountain. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"The ‌falcon", shapes ​the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Wamani ‌in ​ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ‌myths ​of ​Wamani survive ​in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. ‌Each version ​reflects ​the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Wamani ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Wamani ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Incan ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming Wamani, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to sacred ​mountain ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: The ​wamani corrects ‌a ‌flatland habit ​of ​mind. Lowland ​cosmologies ​spread horizontally ​— ‌a tree, ​a ​river, a ‌road; the ​Andes ‌think vertically, ​in ‌the thousand ​metres ​between maize ​and ​snow, and ​the ‌mountain concentrates ​the ‌whole journey ​in ‌one body: ​spring ‌at its ​foot, ‌pasture above, ​ice ​at the ‌crown, ancestors ‌in ‌its caves. ​To ​say 'the ‌mountain ​is my ​grandfather' ‌is not ​metaphor ​but hydrology ‌with ​a face: ‌the ​meltwater that ​feeds ​the terrace ​is ‌his care, ‌the ​drought his ‌displeasure, ​and the ​offering the ‌courtesy ‌owed an ‌elder. ‌The modern ​world ‌is relearning ​this ​grammar late ​— ‌that a ​watershed ​is a ​relationship, ‌that aquifers ​and ​glaciers keep ​accounts ‌— and ​the ‌wamani, whose ​covenant has ‌been ​running since ‌before ‌Cusco, waits ​with ​the patience ​of ​stone for ‌the ‌lesson to ​land.[^1]
